newsitem.title: USA: Oil, gold prices fall, coffee closes the week higher.
newsitem.headline: Oil, gold prices fall, coffee closes the week higher.

text.p: Crude oil prices fell Friday to finished down $2 a barrel for the week with slack demand for heating oil and gasoline leading the market lower.
Gold prices fell to new three-year lows, while coffee prices ended modestly higher.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, March gasoline ended a sharp 2.24 cents lower at 63.06 cents a gallon and March heating oil down 0.92 cent at 60.53 cents a gallon.
March crude oil followed suit and ended 87 cents a barrel lower at $22.23 a barrel.
"We are in the proverbial 'in-between season:' it's too early for gasoline to help the market and it's too late for heating oil," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady.
Heating oil fell more than 8 cents a gallon in the week as temperatures stayed above normal in the northeastern United States, the largest heating oil market in the world.
"Even if it does get cold, refiners can simply dump the inventory they already have on the market," said O'Grady.

Indeed, refiners have more than ample supplies of heating oil, with the American Petroleum Institute reporting this week that distillate stocks, comprised of heating oil and diesel, showed a surplus to year-ago levels for the first time in months.
Some traders also said gasoline imports were expected to approach a strong 650,000 barrels per day in February. However, gasoline demand is traditionally poor in the winter.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee futures ended with gains but off new life-of-contract highs set during the day. March coffee closed at 151.05 cents a pound, up 0.25 cent, after setting a 17-month high at 154.75 cents early.
Expiration of March coffee options Friday and switching of positions by speculators from the March to the May contract contributed to the reduced gains, market sources said.

But worries about short physical supplies that have pushed up prices 50 percent in two months underpinned the market. Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said on Friday that coffee production fell to 778,000 132-pound bags in January compared with 2.08 million bags in January 1996.

"Technically, the market looks terrific," said Victor Henriquez Henriquez, president of Miami-based trading house Hencorp Becstone. "The uptrend is intact. Just close your eyes and buy the dips," he said.
Gold prices fell to new three-year lows on more talk of central bank sales of gold and producer sales.
April gold at the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division ended down $1.10 an ounce at $344, after posting a new contract low at $339.40.
Traders said a seasonal drop in gold demand due to the Moslem holiday of Ramadan and the Chinese New Year holidays this week had also sparked speculative selling by hedge funds.
Demand in Japan also has been dampened by the strength of the dollar, which hit 48-month highs against yen Friday.

"The optimism of a year ago has been replaced by pessimism in a market dominated by fund short selling, intermittent producer panic and central bank liquidation," said CRU International analyst Tony Warwick-Ching.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange March lumber futures closed up the daily limit of $10 per thousand board feet for the second consecutive day, settling at $413.50.

Speculative buying in a thin market aided the rise as talk persisted of a pickup in cash lumber demand. Earlier, the benchmark Random Lengths Framing Lumber Composite index as of Thursday fell $3 for the week to $441, its first drop of 1997.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March wheat closed 2 cents a bushel lower at $3.56 after setting a new contract low of $3.54-1/2 earlier on lack of worry about worldwide supply of wheat this year, traders said.
